title: One rule. A global outage.
subtitle: A firewall rule exhausted CPUs across Cloudflare’s network. The recovery revealed a second problem: the tools to fix it depended on the service that was down.
report: Websites behind Cloudflare returned 502 errors. A newly deployed WAF rule caused excessive regular-expression backtracking and saturated CPUs globally.
evidence: Live CPU inspection, traces and logs pointed to the WAF. Functional tests had passed; they had not measured runaway CPU consumption. Global rule distribution widened the impact.
attempt: Internal access tooling was also affected, slowing the team’s access to recovery controls.
recovery: The team disabled the WAF globally to restore traffic, isolated the problematic rule and restored protection safely.
learning: Test computational cost as well as correctness. Stage globally distributed rules and maintain recovery access independent of the affected service.

title: 43 seconds that changed a day.
subtitle: A short network partition led to a database topology the application could not serve reliably. Restoring service meant protecting writes before chasing speed.
report: A 43-second network partition triggered database failover to a remote region. GitHub experienced degraded service for 24 hours and 11 minutes.
evidence: Both regions held writes that had not replicated. Cross-region application latency was unacceptable, but immediate failback risked data integrity.
attempt: Initial recovery estimates were too optimistic: replicas caught up more slowly under production load. Additional read replicas reduced that pressure.
recovery: GitHub restored backups, synchronized replicas, returned to a stable database topology and processed queued work. Some operations were paused during recovery.
learning: Validate failover against application latency and consistency needs. Exercise restoration at production scale and communicate uncertainty in recovery estimates.

title: When adding capacity wasn’t enough.
subtitle: Network saturation set off a chain of scaling and provisioning failures. Each recovery step needed another part of the system to work.
report: Packet loss during a traffic surge disrupted Slack. Transit Gateway saturation and internal provisioning constraints combined into a wider outage.
evidence: Network waits lowered CPU readings and encouraged downscaling. Later scaling hit provisioning file-descriptor and instance-quota limits; new machines could not serve traffic.
attempt: Rolling back the day’s changes did not help. Some monitoring dashboards were unavailable, although direct metrics queries and logs remained useful.
recovery: Slack disabled downscaling, repaired provisioning and removed broken instances. Web capacity recovered before expanded network capacity resolved the remaining degradation.
learning: Watch dependency saturation alongside CPU. Test how scaling, provisioning and monitoring behave when the network is degraded.

title: The wrong IDs. The right lesson.
subtitle: A maintenance script deleted entire sites instead of an obsolete app. Recovery exposed the difference between restoring one customer and hundreds.
report: A maintenance script used site identifiers where app identifiers were intended. It deleted 883 sites affecting 775 customers.
evidence: Peer review checked the endpoint and procedure but missed the identifier semantics. Standard deletion paths did not trigger the expected outage detection.
attempt: Existing recovery procedures handled individual sites. Restoring hundreds required new automation and parallel recovery work.
recovery: The first sites returned on 8 April; all affected sites were restored by 18 April. The report describes safeguards and disaster-recovery improvements.
learning: Make destructive operations reversible, validate identifier meaning and rehearse recovery at the largest plausible incident scale.

title: A backup is only a promise until restored.
subtitle: An accidental deletion exposed silent backup failures and a slow recovery path.
report: While repairing replication, an engineer removed data on the primary database instead of the secondary. GitLab.com went offline and some recent database changes were lost.
evidence: Logical backups had failed because the dump utility and database versions differed. Failure emails were rejected, and restoration testing had no clear owner.
attempt: The secondary could not provide recovery because it had already been cleared during replication repair. Standard backups were unusable.
recovery: A staging snapshot supplied recoverable data. Slow storage extended copying and restoration; repository and wiki data were stored separately and were not lost.
learning: Give restoration tests an owner. Verify backup outputs and alert delivery, protect destructive commands and measure recovery speed with realistic data volumes.

title: A valid change exposed a hidden bug.
subtitle: A customer configuration activated a latent defect in the edge network.
report: A valid customer configuration triggered a software bug and caused 85% of Fastly’s network to return errors.
evidence: The defect had entered a software rollout on 12 May. It required a specific configuration and circumstances to activate.
attempt: The published summary does not describe an unsuccessful remediation attempt. Detection took one minute; identifying the triggering configuration took longer.
recovery: Fastly disabled the configuration, restoring normal operation to 95% of the network within 49 minutes. Deployment of a permanent software fix began later that day.
learning: A valid configuration can still expose unsafe software behavior. Test combinations of settings and constrain the impact of a single configuration change.

title: The system that everything needed.
subtitle: Two deep performance problems in service discovery turned recovery into a careful sequence of dependencies.
report: Roblox was unavailable for 73 hours after its shared Consul cluster became unhealthy.
evidence: Consul streaming contention and a BoltDB performance pathology combined under unusual load. Dependent monitoring systems lost visibility during investigation.
attempt: Faster hardware, a snapshot reset and reduced service traffic did not independently resolve the problem.
recovery: The team disabled streaming, controlled slow leaders, repaired cache deployment and gradually restored dependent services before admitting players.
learning: Avoid circular recovery dependencies. Test cold startup, keep monitoring independent and reproduce the combination of traffic volume and churn found in production.

title: When redundancy shares the same risk.
subtitle: A maintenance script reached active database machines, including replicas of the same data.
report: A scheduled operating-system upgrade reinstalled active database machines after a script incorrectly classified them as safe. Some primary–replica pairs were affected.
evidence: Remote checks did not reliably identify production state. File contents were separate from the affected metadata databases.
attempt: Replica redundancy could not cover correlated failures. Large databases made conventional backup restoration slow.
recovery: Backups restored most functionality within three hours; core service fully returned on Sunday. Dropbox added local safety checks and parallel binary-log replay.
learning: Require the target machine to reject destructive work when it is active. Test correlated replica failures and large-dataset restore times.

title: Retries that made the queue longer.
subtitle: Internal network congestion impaired both service management and the tools needed to recover.
report: An automated scaling activity triggered a connection surge that overwhelmed devices between AWS internal and main networks.
evidence: Delayed connections caused more retries. A latent client backoff issue sustained congestion; monitoring and deployment tools were also impaired.
attempt: Rerouting internal DNS restored name resolution but did not remove the wider network congestion.
recovery: Operators isolated heavy traffic, disabled some services and added capacity. Network devices recovered by 14:22 PST; individual services and backlogs recovered later.
learning: Test retry behavior under overload. Keep recovery tooling usable during control-plane impairment and distinguish running workloads from resource-management availability.

title: A label change with a wide reach.
subtitle: An undocumented networking dependency made a tested Kubernetes upgrade fail in production.
report: A Kubernetes upgrade disrupted networking in a critical legacy cluster, affecting most Reddit user flows.
evidence: Calico route-reflector selectors depended on a node label removed by the upgrade. This special configuration was not recorded in version control.
attempt: Restarting components and removing a failing admission webhook did not restore the cluster. Recovery instructions also needed updates during the incident.
recovery: The team restored the control plane from backup. The precise route-reflector dependency was understood after service restoration.
learning: Inventory configuration outside standard deployment tools. Test the production topology and keep restore procedures aligned with the current runtime.

title: The network that recovery needed.
subtitle: A backbone command also removed the paths engineers needed to restore service.
report: A maintenance command disconnected the global backbone. An audit-tool defect failed to block it.
evidence: DNS servers withdrew BGP advertisements when datacenters became unreachable, although DNS itself was running.
attempt: Normal and out-of-band access failed. DNS loss also broke internal investigation tools; secure physical access took time.
recovery: Onsite engineers restored the backbone, then controlled service startup to avoid overwhelming caches and power systems.
learning: Exercise independent recovery access and global failure drills. Validate command safeguards and the load of cold recovery.
timeline: Services brought back with controlled load
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval

title: One zone down, one disk degraded.
subtitle: A routine upgrade combined with weak storage and cold caches to overload authentication.
report: Authentication failed during an OS upgrade of the ScyllaDB cluster.
evidence: One zone was offline; another had a degraded disk and cold row caches. Client retries amplified overload.
attempt: Disabling typing and read events improved availability only partially. Immediate node restarts risked breaking quorum.
recovery: The upgrading zone returned at 11:41 PST; sequential restarts restored service by 11:43. Discord expanded capacity and replaced degraded disks.
learning: Check cache readiness and disk health before advancing maintenance. Leave capacity for an additional failure and bound retry load.
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval

title: Separate regions, one hidden trigger.
subtitle: A legacy update schedule bypassed staged deployment and disrupted several regions together.
report: An automatic security update restarted systemd-networkd, deleting Cilium-managed routes and disconnecting nodes across five regions.
evidence: The failure required restarting networking on running nodes; normal boot order did not reproduce it. A legacy update channel synchronized impact.
attempt: Recovery required rebuilding capacity before processing real-time traffic and historical backlog; web access returned before all services.
recovery: Datadog restored services, backfilled data, disabled the redundant update channel and changed networkd configuration to preserve routes.
learning: Audit every update path and test in-place service restarts. Report live-service recovery separately from historical-data completeness.
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval

title: Zero reported usage, real dependency.
subtitle: An incomplete quota migration reduced the capacity of a shared identity service.
vendor: User ID Service / quota automation / Paxos
report: Google services requiring user OAuth authentication became unavailable. Cloud service accounts continued operating.
evidence: Old quota logic reported zero usage; expiry of a grace period reduced database quota, blocked writes and made authentication reads stale.
attempt: Cached errors and service backlogs extended some symptoms after identity recovery. Support tooling was also impaired.
recovery: Engineers disabled quota enforcement in one datacenter, then globally; authentication errors normalized by 04:33 Pacific.
learning: Test migration overlap and zero-load safeguards. Separate identity recovery from downstream recovery, and keep customer communications usable.
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval

duration: Origin repaired same day; caches up to 24 hours
title: The troubleshooting permission that remained.
subtitle: An old permission change left a public SDK artifact writable.
report: An attacker modified the publicly hosted TaskRouter v1.20 SDK. Twilio Flex used a different bundled SDK and was unaffected.
evidence: The S3 path permitted public writes after a build-troubleshooting change. Twilio reported no evidence of customer-data access, not proof of zero individual impact.
attempt: Replacing the origin file did not immediately remove copies from CDN and browser caches.
recovery: Twilio restricted bucket permissions, replaced the artifact and audited other buckets. Affected downloaded copies required replacement.
learning: Expire temporary permissions, verify artifact integrity and account for cached distribution during remediation.
affectedOrganization: Users of TaskRouter JS SDK v1.20
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval

duration: Two account locks over three days
title: An unlock without the missing safeguard.
subtitle: A false positive returned because the first support intervention did not update automation.
report: DigitalOcean identified Raisup as the customer whose legitimate compute activity triggered account locks and resource shutdowns.
evidence: High CPU use and absent payment history triggered anti-fraud automation. The initial unlock omitted the required safety flag.
attempt: Automation locked the account again; a later review incorrectly denied reactivation, extending the disruption.
recovery: Further escalation restored access and resources and applied the safeguards. DigitalOcean proposed peer review and improved support escalation.
learning: Record why an exception was approved and update the mechanism that caused it. Prioritize account-lock appeals and preserve context across responders.
reviewMethod: AI-assisted primary-source reading; not independent incident confirmation or human operational approval
